summary:
Bretagne stands under the national framework of France. Identity-document law, anti-discrimination provisions, criminal law, the prison-placement rules and the marriage statute apply across the country's regions without territorial variation, and no source in the inventory records a Bretagne-specific finding on transgender travellers.

The documented risks concentrate in two settings: custody and the border. In ordinary movement through accommodation, services and public space, France's own oversight bodies record persistent discrimination rather than legal prohibition.

Prison placement follows the sex inscribed on the detainee's identity documents. Article D248 of the French Criminal Procedure Code requires men and women to be held in separate establishments, and the vast majority of trans women, most of whom have not undergone sex-reassignment surgery, carry documents marked male, so they are placed in men's facilities. A BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 records a detainee recalling inmates shouting "We don't want any women here!" alongside threats of violence. Adeline Hazan, controller-general of places of deprivation of liberty, states that transgender detainees, overwhelmingly women, are the group that suffers the most in prison; the feature illustrates this with the case of American trans woman Kara B., held in conditions described as worrying.

The CGLPL, France's national preventive mechanism, issued an opinion of 25 May 2021 on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty, following its opinion of 30 June 2010. It records the persistence of serious violations of trans detainees' fundamental rights in adult prisons, while noting that none were observed in mental-health establishments, closed educational centres or juvenile detention centres. The review covered roughly forty transgender detainees, with interviews including eight trans women and one trans man, and inspection visits at the Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse-Seysses prisons and the Toulouse central police station.

At entry points, trans women have faced questioning of their identity documents in public. Giovanna Rincon's first-person account in StreetPress of 7 March 2017 describes ten minutes of routine humiliation by French border police at the airport, questioned in front of other travellers, documenting identity-document friction for trans travellers arriving in France.

The Défenseur des droits issued a new framework decision on trans rights, confirming persistent fundamental-rights violations drawn from case files and association testimony. It cites the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey, in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination, and sets out official guidance for service providers.

For partner recognition, the legal baseline dates from the marriage-equality law in force by late May 2013; CNN reported France's first same-sex wedding on 29 May 2013, performed days after the law took effect.
tangentialFactors:
The national pattern on prison placement is illustrated by named establishments outside Bretagne: the CGLPL's 2021 inspection visits took in Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse-Seysses prisons and the Toulouse central police station. These are examples of the wider national practice, not findings about facilities in Bretagne.

Placement remained contested years after the 2021 opinion. Louna, a trans woman detained for opposing the A69 motorway works, has been held since mid-October 2024 in the Tarbes men's prison and kept in isolation since October; her incarceration was raised in oral question no. 219 in the French National Assembly, arguing that the case exposes a prison system unable to guarantee conditions for trans detainees.

The 2021 opinion followed the 2016 legal gender-recognition reform, yet the CGLPL recorded no marked improvement since its 2010 opinion, and it extended its coverage to intersex and non-binary detainees. Accounts collected in the BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 describe heightened assault vulnerability and suicide risk under isolation arrangements, and the CGLPL identifies structural problems in the isolation of vulnerable detainees and in suicide prevention.
localsOnly:
Residents held in places of deprivation of liberty are assigned according to the gender inscribed on their identity documents, with each facility improvising: special units, or isolation that restricts contact with other inmates. Treatment varies between establishments.

The CGLPL examined roughly 40 referrals from trans detainees since 2010, together with ministry and association input, and issued binding guidance for places of deprivation of liberty. Its findings rest on a decade of letters from detained trans people.

The national preventive mechanism explained to the Association for the Prevention of Torture that a new opinion was needed because the 2010 opinion produced no marked improvement, because the gender-recognition law and its terminology had changed, and because coverage now extends to intersex and non-binary detainees.

Discrimination on the basis of gender identity is documented in everyday services: the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey found that 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination, and the Défenseur des droits sets out official guidance for service providers drawing on case files and association testimony.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory records a Bretagne-specific finding on transgender travellers; the region's profile rests entirely on the national framework, and this is stated as an absence of regional data rather than as evidence of better or worse conditions in Bretagne.

The BuzzFeed News feature and the CGLPL's 2021 opinion describe conditions at named establishments outside Bretagne. Whether the same placement and isolation practices operate at facilities within Bretagne is not sourced here.

The Défenseur des droits framework decision and the 2023 EU Fundamental Rights Agency survey figures are cited through the parent-framework layer; the full text of the framework decision and its date are not reproduced in this inventory.

The status of Louna's placement after oral question no. 219 is unresolved in the sources provided; the inventory records that her case remains under parliamentary scrutiny without an outcome.
